questions.title: Why do exponential gates let xLSTM revise earlier storage decisions better than sigmoid gates?
questions.question_body: In the xLSTM paper, one of the main claims is that replacing standard sigmoid gating with exponential gating helps fix the LSTM's inability to revise storage decisions. The paper motivates this with a nearest-neighbor search task, where a later token may need to overwrite an earlier stored value if it is a better match. I do not see the mechanism clearly. In a standard LSTM, the update is $c_t = f_t c_{t-1} + i_t z_t$ with $f_t, i_t \in (0,1)$, while in sLSTM the input gate is $i_t = \exp(\tilde{i}_t)$ and the forget gate can also be exponential. Why does making the gates unbounded help the model overwrite or reweight past content more effectively? Is the key point that the ratio between new and old contributions can become arbitrarily large, whereas sigmoid gates cap that ratio?

questions.title: What exactly is the sLSTM normalizer state $n_t$, and why is the hidden state defined as $h_t = o_t (c_t / n_t)$?
questions.question_body: The sLSTM introduces an extra recurrence $n_t = f_t n_{t-1} + i_t$ and then uses $\tilde{h}_t = c_t / n_t$ before output gating. I am confused about what $n_t$ is supposed to represent. If I unroll the recurrence, it looks like both $c_t$ and $n_t$ accumulate past terms with the same gate products, so $c_t / n_t$ seems like some kind of weighted average of past inputs $z_\tau$. Is that the correct interpretation? If so, why is that preferable to the usual LSTM approach of applying something like $\tanh(c_t)$ to keep the state bounded?

questions.title: Why does the stabilization state $m_t$ not change the forward output or gradients in xLSTM?
questions.question_body:
For numerical stability, the paper defines a stabilizer state
$ m_t = \max(\log(f_t) + m_{t-1}, \log(i_t)) $
and then replaces the gates by
$ i'_t = \exp(\tilde{i}_t - m_t) $
and
$ f'_t = \exp(\log(f_t) + m_{t-1} - m_t) $.
The authors say that replacing $i_t, f_t$ by $i'_t, f'_t$ does not change either the network output or the derivatives with respect to the parameters. I can believe this is some kind of rescaling trick, but I do not see it formally. Is the idea that both $c_t$ and the normalizer get multiplied by the same accumulated factor, so the ratio stays unchanged? And if that is the argument, why do the gradients also remain exactly the same rather than just approximately the same?

questions.title: If the forget gate can be $\exp(\tilde{f}_t) > 1$, how is it still a forget gate rather than an amplification gate?
questions.question_body: In a standard LSTM, the forget gate is in $(0,1)$, so it is easy to interpret as decaying old memory. In xLSTM, the forget gate can optionally be exponential, so it can exceed $1$. That seems to mean the old state can be amplified instead of forgotten. Is that intentional? If yes, how should I interpret the term "forget gate" in this setting? Also, what stops the recurrence from becoming unstable if the model repeatedly chooses $f_t > 1$ over many time steps?

questions.title: How is the mLSTM retrieval formula derived, especially the denominator $\max\{ |\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|, 1 \}$?
questions.question_body:
The mLSTM retrieves memory using
$ \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t / \max\{ |\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|, 1 \} $,
where $\mathbf{n}_t = f_t \mathbf{n}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{k}_t$. I understand the numerator somewhat: $\mathbf{C}_t$ is a sum of outer products, so multiplying by a query should mix stored values according to key-query similarity. But I do not understand the denominator. Why should the correct normalization depend on $\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t$ rather than, say, a norm of $\mathbf{q}_t$ or a softmax-like normalizer? And why do they take the absolute value and lower-bound it by $1$?

questions.title: Why does an outer-product update $\mathbf{C}_t = \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$ store key-value pairs at all?
questions.question_body:
The paper motivates mLSTM as an associative memory that stores a key $\mathbf{k}_t$ and value $\mathbf{v}_t$ by adding the outer product $\mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$ to a matrix memory. Later, retrieval is done by multiplying with a query $\mathbf{q}$. If I expand this, I get
$ \mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q} = \sum_\tau \mathbf{v}_\tau (\mathbf{k}_\tau^\top \mathbf{q}) $,
so the result is a weighted sum of all stored values, not the exact value of a single matching key. Is the claim only approximate retrieval under near-orthogonality assumptions on the keys? If so, what role does the paper's assumption of zero-mean normalized keys play in reducing interference terms?

questions.title: In what sense is mLSTM fully parallelizable if its state update is still recurrent?
questions.question_body:
The mLSTM recurrence is written as
$ \mathbf{C}_t = f_t \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top $
and
$ \mathbf{n}_t = f_t \mathbf{n}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{k}_t $.
At first glance this still looks sequential in time, because each state depends on the previous one. The paper says that, unlike sLSTM, mLSTM can be reformulated in a parallel version. Is this basically a prefix-scan over time, similar to how some linear attention or state-space models are parallelized? If yes, what exact property makes mLSTM parallelizable while sLSTM is not? Is it only the absence of hidden-to-hidden memory mixing?

questions.title: What do the authors mean by 'memory mixing', and why is it supposed to matter for state tracking?
questions.question_body: The paper repeatedly contrasts sLSTM and mLSTM by saying that sLSTM has memory mixing and mLSTM does not, and then connects memory mixing to state tracking tasks like parity or formal languages. I am not sure I understand what counts as memory mixing here. Is it specifically the recurrent dependence of the gates and candidate update on the previous hidden state, such as terms like $r_i h_{t-1}$ or $\mathbf{R}_i \mathbf{h}_{t-1}$? If so, why does that make the model fundamentally more expressive for state tracking than architectures that only maintain a linear recurrent state or attention-style memory?

questions.title: Why are multiple heads and multiple cells equivalent for mLSTM but not for sLSTM?
questions.question_body: The paper says that for mLSTM, multiple heads and multiple memory cells are equivalent, while for sLSTM they are not because sLSTM allows memory mixing within a head. I do not see this equivalence clearly. If an mLSTM head has its own matrix memory, output gate, key/query/value projections, and no interaction with other heads, then I can imagine concatenating several such heads. But why is that the same as having multiple cells? Is the claim only about representational structure, or also about parameter count and computation? A concrete explanation with dimensions would help.

questions.title: Why does xLSTM use post up-projection for sLSTM blocks but pre up-projection for mLSTM blocks?
questions.question_body: In the architecture section, the paper says that sLSTM blocks use a residual block with post up-projection, while mLSTM blocks use pre up-projection. The argument references Cover's theorem and says that for mLSTM the memory capacity becomes larger in the high-dimensional space. I am having trouble connecting those ideas. Why is it better to summarize the past in the original space for sLSTM but in the expanded space for mLSTM? Is this a theoretical consequence of the different memory structures, or mainly an empirical design choice that happened to work better?

questions.title: Is mLSTM fundamentally different from linear attention or RetNet, or mostly a gated reparameterization of the same idea?
questions.question_body: The mLSTM equations look very similar to several linear-attention-style models: there is a recurrent matrix state that accumulates outer products, a query-based readout, and a normalization term. The related work section also mentions Retention, Linear Transformer, RWKV-5/6, and HGRN2 as using similar covariance-style updates. So what is the conceptual difference between mLSTM and those models? Is the novelty mainly the LSTM-style gating and how it is integrated into a residual stack, or is there a deeper distinction in what functions the model can represent?

questions.title: Why is only the key projection scaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$ in mLSTM, but not the query projection?
questions.question_body:
In the mLSTM definition, the paper uses
$ \mathbf{k}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_k $,
while the query is simply
$ \mathbf{q}_t = \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_q $.
In Transformer attention, I am used to seeing the dot product $\mathbf{q}^\top \mathbf{k}$ scaled, not just the key. Is this choice equivalent in expectation, or is there a specific reason to scale only the keys here? I am wondering whether this is meant to keep the outer-product memory update $\mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$ at a stable magnitude.

questions.title: When the paper says xLSTM has constant memory complexity in sequence length, does that apply to training or only inference?
questions.question_body: The paper states that, contrary to Transformers, xLSTM has linear computation and constant memory complexity with respect to sequence length. I can understand this at inference time, since the recurrent state size does not grow with context length. But during training, backpropagation through time usually requires storing activations for every time step, which sounds like memory growing with sequence length anyway. So is the claim about constant memory complexity only about the model state during inference, or are the authors assuming checkpointing/recomputation or a custom training algorithm?
